title: There is always one person who plans the trip
excerpt: A short guide for the one who checks dates, flights and everyone's preferences.
subtitle: A short guide for the one who checks dates, flights and everyone's preferences.
author: Eagle Ray Comms Team
body:
![Sailing with friends organizing sailing trip](https://res.cloudinary.com/bsvjo1mn/image/upload/f_auto,q_auto/eagleray-web/brandon-hoogenboom-YuKzs8bFhIs-unsplash_fjt960.jpg)

In every group there is someone who ends up holding the spreadsheet. Comparing dates, triangulate with the flights, ask who can come, who can't and who hasn't answered yet.

Then they do it again when someone changes their mind. It takes time, and it is not always thanked.

It also pays off. The moment the plan clicks and you know it suits your people, all of it is worth it. The trick is to make that moment come sooner, and with less effort. Here is how.

### Decide in this order

People first, then dates, then flights, then everything else.

The usual mistake is to book the first thing that is available and adapt the group to it. Do it the other way round: who is coming decides the dates, the dates decide the flights, and only then do you choose where you sleep and how you travel.

![Planning the sailing trip with friends](https://res.cloudinary.com/bsvjo1mn/image/upload/f_auto,q_auto/eagleray-web/dominik-sostmann-44kbHMzHWmE-unsplash_mmng6y.jpg)

1\. A window, not a date

Offer two or three possible weeks. The more rigid the date, the more people drop out, and every drop-out sends you back to the start. A window lets people answer with "this one works" instead of "I'll check".

2\. Who is really coming

The number of people shapes everything that follows: the type of boat, how many cabins you need, how much each person pays. Ask for a yes or a no, not a "probably". "Probably" is the answer that costs you the most weeks.

3\. A range per person, not a total

"Around X each" is easier to say yes to than "the trip costs Y". It also lets people tell you early if it is out of reach, without having to explain themselves in the group chat.

4\. What the days should feel like

This is the question that changes the most, and the one that is asked the least. Some groups want to do something from morning to night. Others want long lunches and nothing planned. Most are a mix, and the mix is where disagreements start.

Two questions help: what is one thing you do not want to miss, and what is one thing you would rather not do? Two answers from each person tell you more than a list of preferences.

(Imagen: dos momentos opuestos en una misma foto o en un par de fotos. Alguien en el agua, alguien leyendo a la sombra.)

5\. A date to decide

Without one, "let's see" can last months, and prices and availability do not wait. Set a date after which the plan is closed and the group decides with what it has.

How to run the group chat

One question at a time. Close each vote before opening the next one. Do not ask for opinions on everything, only on what actually changes the plan. And agree early on what happens if someone drops out: who covers the difference, or whether the plan simply shrinks.

(Imagen: móvil con un chat de grupo, desenfocado, sin texto legible.)

We think about this person a lot. They are the first to read everything and the last to relax.
